## [0.20.0] - 2026-08-20

The **contracts and certificates release**. Two long-running moves finish. Everything that reads a document - an OpenAPI spec, a Postman collection, an Insomnia export - now reads it in the engine, so there is exactly one opinion about what a document says: the reader, both indexes, operation matching, request drafts, the sync diff, spec export and every import parser move out of the renderer, and an MCP agent can bind a collection to a spec, ask whether the contract has drifted, apply that drift under a policy that will not overwrite a person's edits, export a spec and import a document. Alongside it, client-certificate (mTLS) support grows a per-host registry that answers for every subdomain, ships PKCS#12 as well as PEM, and runs on one OpenSSL backend the engine names for itself on all three platforms, so Windows gets a working mutual-TLS handshake for the first time. The app adds a system proxy mode with a connection test, and a collection run's step list gains search, a way back from a step to the request that produced it, and the ability to scale to thousands of steps. The shape of the release is that move: the engine grows about 10,000 lines of new C++ while the renderer sheds roughly 7,700 net, most of it parsers and comparators that now have a single home.

### Added

- **The OpenAPI stack runs engine-side, end to end.** The engine could not read a stored document at all, so every question about one was answered twice - once by the renderer's parsers and once by whatever the engine derived - and two readers disagree exactly where it matters. `core/openapi_document` is now the one translation unit that includes a YAML library, and rapidyaml (`ryml`) was picked by measurement against js-yaml, the reader the importer already used: it matches on every corpus file, keeps document order, and parses a 2.9 MB / 4,000-operation spec in 33 ms, where yaml-cpp turns the string `"2.0"` into the number 2.0 (which is what Swagger detection reads) and fkYAML sorts mapping keys. Scalars are typed by js-yaml's core schema, anchors, aliases and merge keys expand the way js-yaml expands them, a duplicate mapping key is refused, and expansion is bounded at one node per input byte - without which a 300-byte alias bomb reads for 7.9 seconds and gigabytes. On that reader: `spec_documents.operations` is derived on every write and refused in the body, so the index is a fact about the stored bytes the way `hash` is; the response schema index is derived off the same single walk, including OpenAPI 3.0's schema dialect translated to JSON Schema and a response object that is itself a `$ref`; `POST /specs/match` owns operation matching, ambiguity refused in both directions rather than guessed at; the engine can answer, for a stored document, the requests an import of it would build - method, URL, params, headers, sampled body and the folder each is filed under - off the same walk the indexes come from, which is what the sync diff compares a stored request against field by field; `POST /specs/describe` answers a picked document's format, title and operations so the bind preview and the bind commit read the same bytes through the same reader; `POST /specs/bind` does the whole bind in one transaction, matching the subtree itself and clearing the stamps a re-bind orphans; `POST /specs/diff` is the sync comparison, reading the bound document from the binding and walking the collection's subtree itself, because the three-way user-touched rule is worth nothing if the caller can supply the previous side; and `POST /specs/export` assembles the document, patching a bound collection's own stored bytes rather than regenerating (a regenerated document silently drops every security scheme, vendor extension and description Vayu has no model for) and inventing nothing for an unbound one. Each move is pinned to the renderer's own answers by a cross-language conformance fixture rather than to its code, because a draft the two sides build differently reads as "the document changed this request" on a document nobody edited.
- **Every import format is parsed by the engine, and an agent can import a document.** `POST /import/apply` took a parsed tree and the four parsers that built one lived in the renderer, which left an agent able to bind, describe, diff, sync, export and unbind a spec and unable to import anything. All four formats move: OpenAPI 2.0/3.x, Postman Collection v2.0/v2.1, the Postman environment and globals exports, and Insomnia v4. The OpenAPI half does not get a second reader - it is the same walk the sync diff compares against - and the JavaScript semantics both sides rest on (`??` falling through `null` alone, truthiness, `JSON.stringify`'s number spelling) move into shared engine code rather than being copied. Three routes: `POST /import/parse` reads a raw document and answers the whole result, detecting by content in the order the renderer's detectors ran; `POST /import` parses and applies in one transaction for a caller with no preview to show, with globals written last because that write replaces the whole set and must not run ahead of one that can still fail; and `POST /import/document` hands back a document as a JSON DOM for the one caller that needs a tree to rewrite external `$ref`s. Every parser under `app/src/services/importers/` is deleted and `js-yaml` leaves production `src/`. A 15-document conformance corpus, recorded from the renderer's parsers at the last commit that had them, asserts the engine matches on every build.
- **An agent can ask whether a contract has drifted, and apply the drift without choosing which of it.** `diff_spec` relays the engine's added / removed / changed / unchanged / unmapped answer for a re-fetched document, reading only - nothing stored, no binding moved, no request stamped - so an agent may ask about a document it has not decided to apply, with the write toggle off. Each bucket is capped at 50 entries while the summary carries the engine's true totals, so a document that renamed every operation comes back described rather than whole and a count read off a cut list cannot understate a drift. Applying it is `POST /specs/sync` with `policy: "safe"`: the selection rule that decides what a sync writes when nobody has ticked anything is now `core::safe_spec_apply` rather than renderer-only code, and it is the one judgement whose silent failure destroys a person's work - never write a field somebody edited, never delete by default, leave a request nothing can be told apart about alone. `POST /specs/diff` reports it per entry as `safe` / `safeFields`, so the Spec tab's pre-ticked boxes and a caller with no checkboxes are one answer, and `skipped` counts what the policy declined, because a call answering only with what it wrote reads as "applied the drift". A user who changes a tick still sends explicit rows: a choice a person made is not a policy. Beside those, `get_spec` answers what a collection is bound to, where the document came from and when it was fetched, off the metadata route rather than the document (a real spec runs to megabytes); `unbind_spec` resets the binding and leaves the recorded operation identities alone; `bind_spec` binds from bytes with no pairing supplied; `export_spec` reads a document back out capped at 32 KB with its true size beside it; and `import_document` covers the import.
- **mTLS works on all three platforms, wildcards a host, and ships PKCS#12.** Windows built libcurl against Schannel, whose client-certificate path in curl 8.21 cannot complete a handshake with an identity read from a file, so mutual TLS was simply unavailable there. curl now pins the `openssl` feature with `default-features: false`, which is load-bearing: without it the port's default `ssl` feature keeps Schannel on and the result is a MultiSSL build where the backend a transfer uses is whichever libcurl picked, or whichever a leftover `CURL_SSL_BACKEND` in the environment names. So the engine names its own backend - `pin_tls_backend()` calls `curl_global_sslset` before `curl_global_init`, since curl answers too-late once initialized - and the assertion checks that this process selected it rather than that only one was compiled in. An OpenSSL build on Windows has no CA file to fall back to, so `CURLSSLOPT_NATIVE_CA` is set unconditionally there; without it a user who has pasted nothing would trust nothing at all, and every custom-CA test would have stayed green while it happened. On top of that: a registered certificate's `host` now takes one wildcard pattern read as a label suffix, so an estate behind one mTLS gateway needs one row rather than a row per service - `*.example.com` answers for `api.example.com` and `a.b.example.com`, never for `example.com` itself, never for `notexample.com`, and never for an address literal, because without that last guard `*.0.1` would present the user's identity to `127.0.0.1`. Once two rows can match one transfer, matches are ranked and the maximum taken (closest host first, then port), and the Settings card prints per row what the entry will and will not match, for exact rows too, because a certificate silently not presented is the failure this registry exists to end. A certificate can also go out as PKCS#12 rather than only a PEM pair: the format is a column on the row, the applier writes `CURLOPT_SSLCERTTYPE` on every handle, a declared format that contradicts the file's first bytes is refused, and the card drops the key picker for a bundle instead of demanding a file the format does not have.
- **System proxy, a connection test, and proxy failures that read as proxy failures.** The two networking stacks are disjoint - Chromium resolves the OS proxy for the shell, libcurl carries every request and sees none of it - and the Electron main process is the only place both are visible, so a new `proxyMode: system` resolves through `session.resolveProxy` and writes the answer into a visible setting rather than a hidden channel, refreshed at startup, on resume, and when the renderer comes back online. PAC resolves once against a probe URL and applies engine-wide; a headless engine with nothing resolved falls back to `environment` rather than `off`. `POST /diagnostics/connection` sends one policy-honouring HEAD and answers with which hop refused - proxy, TLS, timeout, other, or ok - plus the proxy in force and the certificate that answered, and it never returns the body, headers or redirect chain, which a test asserts: it is a diagnostics surface, not a second fetch. A Connection test card renders it under Network & connectivity. A proxy error now gets its own heading, icon and a hint naming the setting instead of reading as a generic transport failure, and the SSL hint names both legitimate outs. A pasted curl command now also names the flags it could not import - `-x`, `--cert`, `--cacert` and the rest - in one dismissible notice pointing at the setting that owns each intent, derived from the parsers' own skip sets so a flag that later gets mapped leaves the ledger with no edit.
- **A collection run's step list is navigable and scales.** The step card was a dead end: the engine stamped a `requestId` onto every step trace and no renderer read it, so reproducing "iteration 501 failed" meant finding the request by name and then discovering the send-with-row picker lists the first 20 rows, which do not include row 501. A step now carries a **Repro row N** action that opens the request and binds the row it ran, the picker takes any row by number rather than only one it browses (a number the file has no row for is refused), and the live step frame carries the same id, so the link works while the run streams rather than only after it ends - which is the moment it is worth least, since the reader watching iteration 12 of a 500-iteration run fail had to wait the run out to reach the failure. The list itself used to mount every stored step as a card, up to `maxScenarioStoredSteps` = 5,000 of them; rows now arrive through a growing window, each card marked to cost no layout once scrolled past. Deliberately not a virtualiser: step cards vary in height, and variable-height windowing means a scroll map to maintain forever. The four count chips become filters - the reader who has just read "11 failed" wants those eleven, and the number is where they read it - and a search box beside them matches the step name, which is what a 5,000-step run of a 40-request collection actually needs, since the chips cannot answer "show me every execution of POST /checkout". It matches the name and nothing else, stated on the field and in the docs, because a row's URL lives in its stored trace and a live row has none, so matching it would make the same box search less during a run than after it. Both controls are one predicate, and there is a single empty state naming whichever combination emptied the list, since a reader told "no failed steps" over a list their search emptied clears the wrong control.

### Changed

- **Engine startup opens the database the way the engine means to.** WAL and `synchronous` were applied in `init()`, which runs after the constructor's two schema passes, so every database Vayu has ever opened wrote its schema on SQLite's defaults - a rollback journal at `synchronous=FULL` - which was not a durability choice anyone made but the gap between opening the file and reading the row that says how to open it. The pragmas move into the connection's construction, and the sixty-odd default config rows are seeded in one transaction instead of sixty-odd, which also makes the seed atomic rather than merely self-repairing on the next start.
- **The engine precompiles its two big single-header dependencies, on the platforms where that helps.** `nlohmann/json.hpp` is included in 93 of 174 engine translation units and `httplib.h` in 24, and neither was precompiled. Both now are, on non-MSVC platforms only: measured over consecutive CI runs, sccache silently stops caching `/Yu`-bearing compiles under MSVC - only 48 of 222 build steps reached it as tracked requests, and the warm run came out slower than the cold one - while ubuntu and macOS went from a cold run to a warm one at 97-99% hits, roughly 6-15x faster. Windows keeps its pre-PCH behaviour rather than regressing.
- **A sync states the decision it actually has about examples.** `POST /specs/sync` used to take example rows from the client, which were the engine's own answer read off the diff two calls earlier and echoed back - a round trip that let a payload write examples for responses the document does not describe. The payload now carries `examples: true` to refresh a request's imported examples from the document being stored, absent to leave every one of them alone; a created request always gets the responses its operation documents. The rows come off the same read the indexes come off, so one read of the stored bytes answers everything the route says about them, and a refresh for a request the stored document does not declare is refused rather than answered 200 having written nothing. Relatedly, a document with no `info.title` is now described as having none, so the card's "Untitled API" placeholder is reachable; the renderer used to substitute the name an import would have invented for the collection.
- **Internal work with no user-visible surface.** The mTLS tests now complete real handshakes against a server demanding a client certificate rather than registering files holding the bytes `not-a-real-certificate`; the TLS fixture serves a CA-signed CRL so the Schannel revocation check has the document it asks for, which let two loud skips be deleted once a green leg proved them dead; the PKCS#12 fixture is minted with PBES2/AES-256 rather than SHA-1 and 3DES, because a legacy-PBE bundle imports its key where Schannel cannot use it. The Windows test suite runs 4-wide with the tests that open a scratch database sharing a CTest resource lock, instead of serially: a plain `-j4` there measured ~37 minutes against a ~6 minute serial run, because concurrent SQLite commits on Windows cost more than the concurrency returns. Docs corrected in step: the TLS backend spread is two-way rather than three-way (the pinned curl port has no SecTrust feature, so macOS is OpenSSL-backed like Linux, which makes the CA merge the one thing standing between a pasted corporate CA and a silently narrowed trust store there), the Windows application manifest keeps one live dependent and now states the condition under which it retires, and the compare table gains its proxy and certificates row.

### Fixed

- **The app refuses to navigate off itself and denies `window.open`.** The preload re-runs on whatever the main window navigates to, so a navigation to a third-party origin would hand it `window.electronAPI`, and the only thing in front of that was an application-level convention with no layer underneath. A `will-navigate` refusal and a denying window-open handler are installed before the load, so no navigation can land ahead of the guard. The predicate differs by build on purpose: production is a `file:` load where every URL carries the opaque origin "null", so the document is the identity there, while the dev server's origin is exactly the right test.
- **A client-certificate format the Settings card does not recognize reads as itself, not as a crash.** The row badge indexed straight into the format table, so a `certFormat` outside `pem` / `p12` threw and took the whole Settings screen down. The engine refuses to store such a value but still lists a hand-edited row - dropping it from the transport policy and logging it, which is the right behaviour - and that is exactly what hands the card a value it has no entry for. One bad row blanking Settings is a worse failure than the bad row, and it would hide the very thing the user needs to see to fix it.
- **The engine no longer claims a `workers` change needs a restart.** `workers` was seeded wrapped in the restart-required marker and nothing reads it at startup: the run manager reads it at the start of every run and builds that run's event loop from it. One flag told the same falsehood on three surfaces - the Settings chip and its pending banner, the Dock's pending signal, and the MCP config tool's warning - none of which branches per key, so dropping the wrapper is the whole cure, and an upgraded database sheds the flag on its next start.
- **An explicit key written after a merge key overrides it.** `x: {<<: *base, a: 5}` was refused as a duplicate key, because the merge had already put `a` there. js-yaml reads it as `{a: 5}`, and "these are the defaults, except this one" is what writing a key next to `<<` means, from either side of it. A mapping now remembers which keys came from a merge: an explicit key overrides one of those in place, keeping the merged key's position as a JavaScript object does, while a second explicit spelling of the same key is still the error js-yaml refuses.
